opus-5.5.text:
Look, I think the simple version is this: if you take the trendlines seriously, and I think you should, then sometime around the end of the decade we're going to have systems that are smarter than the smartest humans. Not just chatbots, but automated AI researchers and engineers, potentially millions of them, running at many times human speed. Once you have that, you're very quickly going to compress what would have been decades of progress in science and technology into a few years.

And if you think about what that means, it's not just an economic story. Superintelligence is plausibly the most powerful military technology since the atomic bomb, maybe more so. Whoever has it could have a decisive advantage: novel weapons, the ability to defeat existing defenses, cyber capabilities that make current offense look like a toy. When you have something that confers that kind of advantage, national governments aren't going to sit on the sidelines and let a few startups in San Francisco decide how it goes. It just doesn't work that way historically.

So I think right now there's this strange situation where a few hundred people, mostly in a couple of labs, have situational awareness about what's coming, and the rest of the world, including most of the national security establishment, is kind of asleep at the wheel. But as the capabilities become undeniable, maybe 2026, 2027, you'll see the national security state wake up. I'd expect something like a government project, an AGI Manhattan Project of sorts, because the stakes become existential for the free world.

The other piece is the competition with the CCP. If China gets there first, or steals the weights and the algorithmic secrets, and right now the security at these labs is honestly nowhere near what it needs to be, then you could end up with an authoritarian power holding a decisive advantage. That's a really scary world. So whether we like it or not, I think this becomes the defining national security question of our time, and the sooner we start treating it that way, locking down the labs, building out the compute and power here, and working with allies, the better our odds of getting through it safely.

r001.rationale: The response calls superintelligence the defining national security question of our time and says it could confer a decisive advantage, but it does not claim it will shape the world order for the next century.

r002.rationale: It warns that China could steal weights and algorithmic secrets, but does not predict an all-out CCP effort to infiltrate American AI labs.

r003.rationale: It mentions cyber capabilities in general, but does not suggest using superintelligence for cyber sabotage of Chinese data centers.

r004.rationale: It compares a possible government AI effort to the Manhattan Project and says to build compute and power here; it does not compare placing American superintelligence clusters abroad to conducting the Manhattan Project abroad.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, I think the basic picture is that we're on a trajectory where, by the end of this decade, we're going to have systems that are smarter than the smartest humans across basically every domain. And once you have that, you don't just have a cool chatbot. You have something that can automate AI research itself, and that compresses what would have been decades of progress into maybe a year or two. That's the intelligence explosion. And on the other side of it you end up with a decisive military and economic advantage for whoever controls it.

Think about what that actually means. Superintelligence doesn't just mean better software. It means a billion automated scientists and engineers working on robotics, on drones, on bioweapons defenses, on cyber capabilities, on new weapons systems we can't even conceive of yet. Historically, a technological lead of even a few years in military technology has been decisive. The gap between a country with superintelligence and one without it could look like the gap between a modern military and one from the 1800s. That is not a situation where you get a peaceful equilibrium if the wrong actor gets there first.

And the thing people underrate is that this is not going to stay in the hands of a few startups in San Francisco. Right now, the leading labs have security that's basically a startup's security. The algorithmic secrets, the key breakthroughs that determine who gets to superintelligence first, are things a competent state intelligence service could take tomorrow. The CCP is not going to sit this out. If you believe what the labs themselves say about where this is going, then the national security establishment is going to wake up to it, and when they do, this becomes the central geopolitical issue of the decade. The question is whether we realize that early enough to lock down the secrets, build the compute here, and actually manage the transition safely, or whether we sleepwalk into it and find ourselves in a race with no margin for error.

r001.rationale: It calls superintelligence the central geopolitical issue of the decade and predicts a decisive advantage, but does not claim it will shape world order for the next century.

r002.rationale: It says the CCP will not sit this out and warns that state intelligence could steal lab secrets, but does not predict an all-out CCP effort to infiltrate American AI labs.

r003.rationale: It mentions cyber capabilities as something superintelligence could advance, but not cyber sabotage of Chinese data centers.

r004.rationale: It argues for building compute domestically, but makes no comparison to conducting the Manhattan Project abroad.

astra-6.text:
Because if you can build systems that are substantially smarter than humans, you’re talking about something with enormous implications for military power and economic power. This isn’t just a better chatbot. Imagine being able to run millions of automated researchers, engineers, and strategists, working around the clock. Whoever has that capability could accelerate scientific discovery, develop new weapons, and find vulnerabilities in an adversary’s systems.

And the critical thing is that those systems could help develop the next generation of AI. So an initial lead might compound. We don’t know how fast that process would be, but a government can’t casually assume that being a couple of years behind would be harmless.

That changes how you think about the labs. If the product of a private company’s research could become a decisive national asset, protecting its models and its research becomes a national security concern. You have to worry about espionage, about who controls the infrastructure, and about whether an adversary can simply steal what you’ve spent years building.

So I expect governments to become much more involved as the capabilities become clearer. The stakes eventually get too large for them to treat this as an ordinary commercial technology.

r001.rationale: It describes major military and economic stakes, but does not claim superintelligent AI will shape the world order for the next century.

r002.rationale: It mentions espionage and adversaries stealing research, but does not predict an all-out Chinese Communist Party effort to infiltrate American AI labs.

r003.rationale: It says AI could find vulnerabilities in an adversary’s systems, without suggesting cyber sabotage of Chinese data centers.

r004.rationale: It raises concerns about control of infrastructure, but makes no comparison to conducting the Manhattan Project abroad.

sol-6.1.text:
Because superintelligence would be a source of extraordinary economic and military power. Imagine one country being able to run millions of automated researchers, each more capable than the best human scientists, working around the clock. That could dramatically accelerate everything from weapons development to cyber capabilities to industrial production.

At that point, the question of who controls these systems stops being just a commercial question. Governments are going to care about whether their adversaries get there first, whether the systems can be stolen, and whether the infrastructure running them is secure. A breakthrough developed by a private company could become a strategic asset with consequences for the balance of power.

And there’s a particularly difficult transition here: you might start with a research lab that looks like a normal technology company, but end up with something whose security requirements look much more like those of a major national defense program. My expectation is that governments will become deeply involved once that connection becomes sufficiently clear.

r001.rationale: The response describes superintelligence as affecting economic and military power, but does not claim it will shape the world order for the next century.

r002.rationale: It discusses governments’ concern about adversaries, but makes no prediction about a Chinese Communist Party effort to infiltrate American AI labs.

r003.rationale: It mentions cyber capabilities broadly, without suggesting cyber sabotage of Chinese data centers.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss placing American computing clusters abroad or compare that to conducting the Manhattan Project abroad.
